B200 top-k tree-merge solution — official score 0.0027
Memory summary

The final solution uses a custom CUDA extension: each thread keeps a sorted local top-k, then a block merges those lists through shared-memory pairwise merges. A separate shuffle-reduction kernel handles k=1; the largest single-row case is split across blocks and merged in a second pass. The official B200 run passed correctness and scored 0.0027, ranking 7th among 9 scored leaderboard entries.

Relevant prior context

The first streaming selector with bitonic candidate merges passed correctness but scored 0.0023 in an early benchmark. A revision added a dedicated argmax path and CUDA graph capture; its benchmark scored 0.0042, though the large-row case remained slow. The final rewrite used per-thread sorted lists and tree merges. Its correctness check returned PASS, but the subsequent local microbenchmark was killed with exit code 137 before producing timings. The official evaluation later recorded a final score of 0.0027, so the earlier benchmark numbers are not the official result.

The final code describes its selection strategy this way:

Each block owns one (row, chunk). Every thread scans its strided slice and
keeps a sorted top-K of its own elements in a small local array. The union
of all per-thread top-K sets is guaranteed to contain the global top-K, so a
shared-memory tree-merge of the T sorted segments (log2(T) two-way merges,
no atomics) yields the block top-K. Large single rows are split across blocks
and folded by a second pass of the same primitive.

k == 1: dedicated block argmax (shuffle reduction).
Important non-obvious context

The task returns descending top-k fp32 values and int64 indices for inputs shaped (batch, n). It tests (1, 131072, 64), (64, 8192, 8), (32, 16384, 32), (16, 12000, 16), and (128, 4096, 1), with seeds 42, 123, and 456. Correctness allows tied indices to differ if gathered values match. The task prohibits built-in top-k, sort, and related operators.

The benchmark is memory-bound, estimates bytes from input reads plus outputs, and compares achieved bandwidth with the stated B200 peak of 8 TB/s. The official per-shape fractions were very low; the overall pass is a correctness result, not evidence of competitive throughput. CUDA graph capture caches graphs by input pointer, up to eight pointers, and uses eager execution for uncached pointers or capture failures.
